slots.name: Flight computer
slots.role: The computer that flies the ship and how many copies of it there are.

options.name: Single computer
options.note: One flight computer. If it fails, the crew flies by hand.
options.real: Mercury, Gemini

options.name: Triple redundant, voting
options.note: Three computers vote on every command; one can fail without anyone noticing.
options.real: Dragon, Soyuz

options.name: Four plus a backup
options.note: Four identical computers and a fifth with different software, as the Shuttle flew.
options.real: Space Shuttle GPCs

slots.name: Life-support loop
slots.role: Air and water: used once, or recycled.

options.name: Open loop
options.note: Oxygen from tanks, CO₂ into canisters, water from bags. Simple; it lasts as long as the stores do.
options.real: Apollo, Dragon

options.name: Regenerative loop
options.note: Water is split to make the cabin's oxygen and carbon dioxide is cleaned out and reused, as on the ISS: the spare oxygen goes only to the suit. It needs a backup scrubber: if it fails, nothing else cleans the air.
options.real: ISS ECLSS

slots.name: Crew couches
slots.role: What the crew sits in through launch and landing.

options.name: Fixed couches
options.note: Padded seats bolted to the floor.
cons: A hard landing is felt in full
options.real: Mercury contour couch, moulded to each astronaut

options.name: Shock-attenuating couches
options.note: Seats hung on crushable struts that soak up a hard landing.
options.real: Apollo, Orion

options.name: Ejection seats
options.note: Each seat is a small rocket that throws its astronaut clear, then opens a parachute. An escape with no tower, but only low and slow.
options.real: Gemini (usable up to about 4.6 km), Vostok (the cosmonaut ejected on every landing)

slots.name: Windows
slots.role: How much of the wall is glass.

options.name: Small ports
options.note: Two small panes of fused silica. Strong wall, little view.
options.real: Soyuz

options.name: Panoramic windows
options.note: Big triple-pane windows. The view of a lifetime, and a weaker, heavier wall.
options.real: New Shepard, the largest windows flown

options.name: Glass dome in the nose
options.note: A dome of glass where the docking port would be: the widest view ever flown. One big pane in place of many cut-outs.
pros: The whole sky in one window
options.real: Crew Dragon Resilience on Inspiration4 (2021)

slots.name: Hatch
slots.role: Which way the door opens.

options.name: Outward, quick release
options.note: Opens outward in seconds, even against cabin pressure. The rule since 1967.
options.real: Apollo (after Apollo 1), Dragon

options.name: Inward plug hatch
options.note: Cabin pressure seals it tighter. It cannot be opened against that pressure: the Apollo 1 crew died behind one.
cons: Cannot open in a cabin fire
options.real: Apollo 1 (1967)

options.name: Top hatch only
options.note: No door in the side wall: the crew climbs out through the hatch in the nose. No cut-out to reinforce, but a slow way out after landing.
options.real: Soyuz and Shenzhou descent modules

slots.name: Docking port
slots.role: The mechanism on the nose that latches onto another ship or a station and seals a tunnel between them.

options.name: Hatch and tunnel only
options.note: A plain hatch in the nose tunnel and no latching mechanism. Lightest; this ship can never dock with anything.
options.real: Vostok, Voskhod, Mercury and Gemini capsules (Gemini docked with its nose section, not a tunnel)

options.name: Probe and drogue
options.note: A probe on one ship slides into a cone (the drogue) on the other, then twelve latches pull the rings tight. The probe and drogue are removed by hand to open the tunnel.
cons: Only an active ship meets a passive one
options.real: Apollo command module and lunar module (1968–75)

options.name: SSVP probe-cone (Soyuz)
options.note: The Russian probe-and-cone system with a ring of hooks: a probe ship and a cone ship, and an 80 cm tunnel between them once the hooks close.
pros: Flown on every Soyuz and Progress for fifty years
cons: Needs the opposite half on the other ship
options.real: Soyuz and Progress SSVP-G4000 (since 1971); Russian ISS ports

options.name: Androgynous ring (APAS)
options.note: Both ships carry the same ring of three petals, so any two can dock. A soft-capture ring with dampers soaks up the bump.
options.real: APAS-75 (Apollo-Soyuz 1975), APAS-89/95 (Shuttle to Mir and the ISS); China's docking system is APAS-derived

options.name: Low-impact docking ring (NDS / IDSS)
options.note: The international standard: a soft-capture ring on electric actuators reaches out, catches the other port gently and pulls the ships together. The 80 cm tunnel opens straight through.
options.real: NASA Docking System on Orion, Starliner; Crew Dragon's IDSS-compatible port; ISS IDA adapters (2016)

options.name: Berthing ring (CBM)
options.note: A wide square hatch in a ring of bolts. The ship cannot dock itself: it parks next to the station and a robot arm pulls it in. The widest door in space, about 1.27 m.
cons: Needs a robot arm at the other end
options.real: Common Berthing Mechanism: ISS modules, Cygnus, HTV, Dragon 1 (CBM rings 200–311 kg), Dream Chaser

slots.name: Cabin air
slots.role: What the crew breathes, and at what pressure.

options.name: Air at sea-level pressure
options.note: Nitrogen and oxygen at the same pressure as on the ground. A thick wall to hold it, but a fire burns no faster than at home.
options.real: Soyuz, Shuttle, Crew Dragon, Orion

options.name: Pure oxygen at one-third pressure
options.note: Only oxygen, at about 34 kPa. The wall can be thinner and there are no nitrogen tanks, but anything that sparks burns fiercely.
options.real: Mercury, Gemini, Apollo; the Apollo 1 fire (1967) on the pad with pure oxygen above sea-level pressure

options.name: Nitrogen-oxygen on the pad, oxygen in space
options.note: 60 % oxygen and 40 % nitrogen on the ground, bled down to pure oxygen at low pressure after launch. The change NASA made after Apollo 1.
options.real: Apollo command module from Apollo 7 (1968)

slots.name: Launch and entry suits
slots.role: Whether the crew wear pressure suits when the cabin could leak: launch, docking and landing.

options.name: Shirt-sleeves
options.note: Overalls and a headset. Lighter, more room, and no protection if the cabin loses its air.
options.real: Voskhod 1 (1964), Soyuz 1 to Soyuz 11; the Soyuz 11 crew died in 1971 when a valve let the air out during descent

options.name: Pressure suits
options.note: Each crew member wears a suit plugged into the cabin, which inflates if the cabin pressure drops.
pros: Since Soyuz 11 (1971), every Soyuz crew wears them
options.real: Sokol-K (Soyuz 12, 1973) and Sokol-KV2 (from Soyuz T-2, 1980); Shuttle ACES, Crew Dragon IVA suit, Orion crew survival suit

slots.name: Touchdown on Earth
slots.role: How the capsule meets the ground or the sea at the end of the trip home.

options.name: Splashdown
options.note: The capsule hangs under its parachutes and lands in the sea at about 8 m/s; ships pick it up.
options.real: Mercury, Gemini, Apollo, Orion, Crew Dragon

options.name: Soft-landing rockets
options.note: The heat shield drops away and small solid rockets in the base fire about a metre above the ground, slowing the capsule from about 7 m/s to 2.
options.real: Soyuz (since 1967), Shenzhou; Voskhod was the first to use them

options.name: Hard landing on the ground
options.note: The capsule comes down on land under its parachute at about 10 m/s, with nothing to soften the last metre. A helicopter team finds it; no fleet at sea.
options.real: Vostok descent module (1961–63): 574 m² main, 10–12 m/s at touchdown

options.name: Airbags under the capsule
options.note: The heat shield drops away and bags inflate underneath, cushioning a landing on the ground.
options.real: Boeing Starliner (2019, 2022, 2024 landings in New Mexico)

slots.name: Separation
slots.role: How the fairing comes apart once the air is thin.

options.name: Two halves (bisector)
options.note: The fairing splits down the middle and the halves swing away on hinges.
options.real: Falcon 9, Delta II

options.name: Three petals
options.note: Three lighter pieces, each needing its own pushers.
options.real: Titan IV; Delta IV Heavy 5-m metallic trisector

slots.name: Acoustic blankets
slots.role: Padding against the roar of liftoff, which can shake a payload apart.

options.name: None
options.note: Bare composite skin. Loud inside: 140 dB at liftoff.

options.name: Acoustic blankets
options.note: Foam and fibre panels that cut the sound by 10 dB.
options.real: Every modern fairing

slots.name: Release
slots.role: What throws the pieces clear.

options.name: Pyrotechnic
options.note: Explosive bolts and a shaped cord. Sudden and loud.
options.real: Delta II

options.name: Pneumatic pushers
options.note: Gas pistons shove the halves away gently.
options.real: Falcon 9

slots.name: Ablator thickness
slots.role: How much material there is to burn away.

options.name: Standard
options.note: Sized for one entry with margin.

options.name: Thick
options.note: A quarter more ablator for a steep or hot entry.
options.real: Stardust (12.9 km/s entry)

slots.name: Seams
slots.role: How the blocks of shield are joined.

options.name: Gap filler
options.note: Blocks of ablator with a soft filler between them.
cons: Fillers can protrude and trip the flow
options.real: Orion (Artemis I)

options.name: One piece
options.note: The whole shield cast as one block. No seams, hard to make.
options.real: Apollo Avcoat honeycomb

slots.name: Canopy
slots.role: The shape of the chute.

options.name: Disk-gap-band
options.note: The Mars standard: a disk, a gap, a band. Opens supersonic without tearing.
options.real: Viking to Perseverance

options.name: Ringsail
options.note: Rings of sail cloth: more drag per kilogram, but subsonic only (below about Mach 0.7). On Mars that is only about 2 km up: too low to slow a heavy ship alone.
cons: Subsonic only: on Mars it opens about 2 km up
options.real: Apollo, Orion mains

options.name: Conical ribbon
options.note: Bands of tape with gaps between them: air leaks through, so it survives opening at high speed. Less drag.
options.real: Apollo and Orion drogue chutes

options.name: Steerable parafoil
options.note: A ram-air wing of cloth cells that glides and can be steered to a chosen spot. It has never landed a crewed capsule.
cons: Opens only when very slow: on Mars far too low to help alone
options.real: NASA X-38 drop tests (1999–2001); Falcon 9 fairing halves; Gemini's paraglider was tested but never flown

slots.name: Reefing
slots.role: Whether the chute opens in stages.

options.name: Full open
options.note: One hard jerk.
cons: Peak load tears a weak chute

options.name: Staged reefing
options.note: Cutters release the canopy in two steps, halving the peak load.
options.real: Orion, Dragon

slots.name: Ablator thickness
slots.role: How much material there is to burn away.

options.name: Standard
options.note: Sized for one entry with margin.

options.name: Thick
options.note: A quarter more ablator for a steep or hot entry.
options.real: Stardust (12.9 km/s entry)

slots.name: Seams
slots.role: How the blocks of shield are joined.

options.name: Gap filler
options.note: Blocks of ablator with a soft filler between them.
cons: Fillers can protrude and trip the flow
options.real: Orion (Artemis I)

options.name: One piece
options.note: The whole shield cast as one block. No seams, hard to make.
options.real: Apollo Avcoat honeycomb

slots.name: Ablator
slots.role: What the shield is made of: the material that chars and carries the heat away.

options.name: Avcoat in honeycomb
options.note: Silica fibres in epoxy, gunned cell by cell into a fibreglass honeycomb. Chars into a tough crust and carries the heat away.
cons: Slow to make: every cell is filled by hand
options.real: Apollo, Orion

options.name: PICA (carbon ablator)
options.note: Phenolic-impregnated carbon: a light, foam-like carbon block, the best for the fastest entries.
options.real: Stardust (the fastest entry ever flown), Dragon 1 PICA-X, Crew Dragon PICA-3

options.name: SLA-561V (cork and silica)
options.note: Cork and silica in a honeycomb: light and cheap, fine for Mars, too weak for the 11 km/s return to Earth.
options.real: Viking, Mars Pathfinder, Spirit and Opportunity

options.name: Avcoat in moulded blocks
options.note: The same Avcoat, cast in about 186 blocks and bonded on, instead of filling a honeycomb cell by cell. Quicker to build; on its first flight chunks of char broke away between the blocks.
options.real: Orion from Artemis I (2022): 186 blocks; NASA traced the char loss to gas trapped in the Avcoat and changed the entry path for Artemis II

options.name: Fibreglass and phenolic resin
options.note: Layers of glass cloth soaked in resin, built up like plywood. Cheap, tough, heavier than modern ablators.
options.real: Mercury orbital flights (1962–63)

options.name: Silicone elastomer in honeycomb
options.note: A rubbery silicone ablator packed into a glass-fibre honeycomb. It chars into a glassy crust.
options.real: Gemini: Dow Corning DC-325 in a glass-fibre honeycomb

options.name: Boeing Lightweight Ablator
options.note: A light, filled silicone ablator sprayed onto the shield, made for capsules returning from low orbit.
options.real: Boeing Lightweight Ablator on Starliner

options.name: Carbon-phenolic
options.note: Dense carbon cloth in phenolic resin: the toughest ablator there is, for the fastest entries ever flown. Very heavy.
options.real: Galileo probe into Jupiter (1995), Pioneer Venus probes, missile re-entry vehicles

options.name: Beryllium heat sink
options.note: No ablator at all: a thick metal plate soaks up the heat like a frying pan. It only works for a short, slow entry; a fall from orbit would melt it.
cons: Soaks up only a short, slow entry: from orbit it can burn through
options.real: Mercury-Redstone 3 and 4 (1961): beryllium heat sinks on the suborbital flights

slots.name: Escape motor
slots.role: The solid motor that pulls the capsule away.

options.name: Canted nozzles at the base
options.note: A solid motor whose nozzles sit just above the truss, tilted outward so the flame misses the capsule.
cons: The tower must be tall to keep the flame off the cabin
options.real: Apollo launch escape motor: four canted nozzles, about 147,000 lbf (654 kN) for 3.2 s

options.name: Ring of small nozzles
options.note: Many small nozzles round the tower spread the push; one can burn through and the others still carry the cabin.
options.real: Soyuz SAS main motor, up to 76 t (745 kN)

options.name: Reverse-flow motor
options.note: The gas flows up the motor and turns back out through four nozzles near the top: a shorter tower, and the flame starts far from the capsule.
options.real: Orion abort motor, about 400,000 lbf (1.8 MN)

options.name: Low- and high-altitude motors
options.note: Two sets of solid motors: one set for an escape near the ground, a second set tuned for the thin air higher up, plus a jettison motor.
options.real: Gaganyaan crew escape system (TV-D1 test, 21 October 2023)

slots.name: Tower jettison
slots.role: How the tower leaves on a good flight, once the air is thin.

options.name: Separate jettison motor
options.note: A small motor near the top pulls the tower away a couple of minutes after launch.
options.real: Apollo tower jettison motor, 31,500 lbf for 1.1 s; Mercury 1.4-KS-785

options.name: Jettison motor with backup
options.note: If the jettison motor fails to light, the escape motor fires instead: the tower always goes.
options.real: Apollo: the launch escape motor was the backup for tower jettison

options.name: One motor does both
options.note: The escape motor also throws the tower away. Lighter and cheaper, but one failure keeps the tower on.
options.real: Early Soyuz SAS: the same solid motor separated the capsule and, on a normal flight, the tower

slots.name: Steering after an abort
slots.role: What keeps the escaping capsule pointed the right way.

options.name: Ballast in the nose
options.note: A lump of ballast keeps the nose heavy, so the escaping stack flies straight like a dart.
cons: The capsule must turn itself round afterwards
options.real: Mercury: 236 lb (107 kg) of ballast in the tower nose

options.name: Deployable canards
options.note: Two clamshell fins open 11 seconds after an abort and turn the capsule heat-shield first before the tower leaves.
options.real: Apollo: two metal canards about 4 ft long

options.name: Attitude control motor
options.note: A solid gas generator with eight valves round the tower steers the whole escape stack, even right off the pad.
options.real: Orion attitude control motor: up to 7,000 lbf of steering force

options.name: Folding grid fins
options.note: Four lattice fins on the fairing swing out when the tower fires and keep the escaping front end flying straight, like the feathers on a dart.
options.real: Soyuz escape system (saved Soyuz T-10a, 1983); Shenzhou and Gaganyaan escape fairings

slots.name: Engine chambers
slots.role: How the two engines in the pod are made.

options.name: 3D-printed Inconel
options.note: Each chamber is laser-sintered in one piece of nickel superalloy, cooling channels and all. Light and quick to make.
options.real: SuperDraco: 71 kN, the first fully printed engine to fly

options.name: Forged and machined
options.note: Machined from forgings and welded: heavier, but every wall and weld can be inspected.
options.real: Aerojet RS-88, Starliner's launch abort engine

slots.name: Propellant
slots.role: Where the abort engines draw their propellant from.

options.name: Shared with the thrusters
options.note: Hypergolic NTO and MMH from the same tanks as the steering thrusters; an unused abort leaves propellant for manoeuvres.
cons: A leaking thruster could drain the abort
options.real: Crew Dragon

options.name: Own tanks and valves
options.note: The pod keeps its own small tanks: nothing else can drain them.
options.real: Separate abort feed lines, as in Starliner's service module

slots.name: Thruster propellant
slots.role: What the small steering thrusters burn.

options.name: Hypergolic pair
options.note: Two liquids (MMH and nitrogen tetroxide) that ignite on contact: no igniter, thousands of pulses, but both are toxic.
options.real: Apollo, Shuttle, Orion, Crew Dragon (Draco, 400 N)

options.name: Hydrogen peroxide
options.note: One liquid that a silver catalyst breaks into hot steam and oxygen. Simple and clean, but weaker, and it slowly decomposes in its tank.
options.real: Mercury capsule thrusters, Soyuz descent module

options.name: Hydrazine monopropellant
options.note: One liquid split by a hot catalyst bed: simpler than a pair, nearly as strong.
options.real: Most satellites; the Mars Science Laboratory cruise stage and descent stage

options.name: Cold nitrogen
options.note: Nitrogen gas squirted from bottles through valves: nothing burns, so almost nothing can go wrong, but it pushes weakly and the bottles are heavy.
options.real: Vostok attitude control (nitrogen jets on the instrument module), the Manned Maneuvering Unit (1984)

slots.name: Thruster rings
slots.role: How many independent sets of thrusters there are.

options.name: One ring
options.note: One set of thrusters on one set of valves.
cons: A stuck valve has no backup
options.real: Most uncrewed spacecraft

options.name: Two independent rings
options.note: Two separate sets with their own tanks and valves. If one sticks open, the crew shuts it off and steers with the other.
options.real: Gemini: the re-entry control system saved Gemini 8 (1966) when a thruster stuck open; Apollo command module (two rings of six)

slots.name: Power source
slots.role: Where the electricity comes from between launch and the trip home.

options.name: Unfolding solar wings
options.note: Wings of solar cells that unfold in space and turn to face the Sun. Unlimited power in sunlight, batteries in the shadow.
options.real: Soyuz, Shenzhou, Orion European Service Module, ATV, Cygnus

options.name: Cells on the skin
options.note: Solar cells laid flat on the outside of the module: nothing to unfold, but only part of the skin faces the Sun.
options.real: Crew Dragon trunk, Starliner service module, HTV

options.name: Hydrogen-oxygen fuel cells
options.note: Hydrogen and oxygen from cold tanks combine into electricity and drinking water. Steady power in sunlight or shadow, for about two weeks of gas.
options.real: Gemini (first fuel cells in space, 1965), Apollo service module (Apollo 13 lost its oxygen tank), Shuttle

options.name: Batteries only
options.note: Silver-zinc batteries charged on the ground. Light and simple, and they run flat in days.
options.real: Vostok, Voskhod, Mercury

slots.name: Service engine
slots.role: The module's own engine for course corrections and the burn home. The ship's main engines do the big pushing, so here it counts as the backup.

options.name: One main engine
options.note: One pressure-fed engine on two hypergolic liquids, with a ring of small thrusters.
options.real: Apollo SPS (91 kN), Orion OMS-E (a Shuttle OMS engine, 27 kN), Soyuz main engine

options.name: Main engine and a backup set
options.note: A second, smaller set of engines that can do the main engine's job if it fails.
options.real: Orion's eight auxiliary engines, which can stand in for its main engine

options.name: Thrusters only
options.note: No main engine: the capsule's own thrusters do every burn.
options.real: Crew Dragon trunk (Draco thrusters in the capsule), Gemini adapter (16 thrusters)

slots.name: Docking port
slots.role: The mechanism on the nose that latches onto another ship or a station and seals a tunnel between them.

options.name: Hatch and tunnel only
options.note: A plain hatch in the nose tunnel and no latching mechanism. Lightest; this ship can never dock with anything.
options.real: Vostok, Voskhod, Mercury and Gemini capsules (Gemini docked with its nose section, not a tunnel)

options.name: Probe and drogue
options.note: A probe on one ship slides into a cone (the drogue) on the other, then twelve latches pull the rings tight. The probe and drogue are removed by hand to open the tunnel.
cons: Only an active ship meets a passive one
options.real: Apollo command module and lunar module (1968–75)

options.name: SSVP probe-cone (Soyuz)
options.note: The Russian probe-and-cone system with a ring of hooks: a probe ship and a cone ship, and an 80 cm tunnel between them once the hooks close.
pros: Flown on every Soyuz and Progress for fifty years
cons: Needs the opposite half on the other ship
options.real: Soyuz and Progress SSVP-G4000 (since 1971); Russian ISS ports

options.name: Androgynous ring (APAS)
options.note: Both ships carry the same ring of three petals, so any two can dock. A soft-capture ring with dampers soaks up the bump.
options.real: APAS-75 (Apollo-Soyuz 1975), APAS-89/95 (Shuttle to Mir and the ISS); China's docking system is APAS-derived

options.name: Low-impact docking ring (NDS / IDSS)
options.note: The international standard: a soft-capture ring on electric actuators reaches out, catches the other port gently and pulls the ships together. The 80 cm tunnel opens straight through.
options.real: NASA Docking System on Orion, Starliner; Crew Dragon's IDSS-compatible port; ISS IDA adapters (2016)

options.name: Berthing ring (CBM)
options.note: A wide square hatch in a ring of bolts. The ship cannot dock itself: it parks next to the station and a robot arm pulls it in. The widest door in space, about 1.27 m.
cons: Needs a robot arm at the other end
options.real: Common Berthing Mechanism: ISS modules, Cygnus, HTV, Dragon 1 (CBM rings 200–311 kg), Dream Chaser

slots.name: Stowage
slots.role: How the cargo and supplies are packed inside.

options.name: Cargo bags
options.note: Soft cloth bags strapped to the walls: light and they fit anything.
options.real: Cargo transfer bags on every ISS supply ship

options.name: Standard racks
options.note: Metal racks the size of a refrigerator, bolted in, with power and cooling for experiments.
options.real: International Standard Payload Racks (ISS, HTV, Cygnus)

options.name: Water around the walls
options.note: Bags of the trip's drinking water packed against the walls, where they also soak up radiation.
options.real: NASA studies of water and stores as radiation shielding for crews beyond low orbit
